This thesis proposes a multilevel evaluation framework for Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) aimed at comparing model-agnostic explainers under controlled and reproducible benchmarking conditions. To address the evaluation fragmentation in the field, the framework integrates three complementary components: (i) a seven-gate operational protocol (FOM-7) that links experimental design, artifact qualification, and statistically admissible inference; (ii) a multi-metric quantitative benchmark on real-world tabular data evaluating SHAP, LIME, Anchors, and DiCE across five model families; and (iii) a structured taxonomy of XAI evaluation metrics organized along four axes (evaluation target, evidence source, quality property, and task context), which makes three of the field's construct gaps explicit.

The empirical study uses the Adult (UCI Adult Income) dataset and operationalizes five primary metrics: faithfulness, stability, parsimony, faithfulness gap, and computational cost. Confirmatory inference relies on nonparametric comparisons over 15 blocks with multiplicity control and on a paired SHAP-LIME analysis quantifying the quality-cost trade-off. Results show large and consistent differences across methods: SHAP attains the best mean faithfulness and stability, with very large effect sizes over LIME (d_z = 4.82 for faithfulness and d_z = 3.00 for stability), although the advantage is not uniform across model families. LIME remains attractive when latency constraints dominate, at the cost of severe instability under the configuration and feature space evaluated; this is a property of the (configuration, feature space) pair rather than a universal property of the method. Anchors and DiCE address qualitatively different explanatory objectives than feature attribution. A cross-dataset check on two further datasets replicates the SHAP-over-Anchors faithfulness ordering, delimiting the external scope of the findings.

A complementary study evaluates whether language-model judges can sustain the semantic evaluation of explanations. The result is negative: inter-judge agreement, measured as ICC(1,1), ranges from 0.321 to 0.601 depending on the dimension, falling short of the threshold required to support confirmatory claims, which confines such judges to an exploratory, instrument-calibration role. Overall, the thesis contributes a portable protocol, quantified comparative evidence with its validity conditions made explicit, and a conceptual framework to support operationally grounded XAI method selection and reproducible evidence accumulation.
